Expression: a faint knowing smile.
Her element, carried in her design: cobalt: a hard, faintly bluish silver metal named for the kobold, the mischievous goblin of Saxon mines blamed for stealing silver and leaving behind ore that gave off poisonous arsenic fumes in the furnace; melted into glass it gives the deepest, most enduring blue, the blue of blue-and-white porcelain, of smalt and of cobalt-blue paint; its weathered ore blooms in rose-pink crystals, and its salts turn pink when wet and blue when dry; today the heart of rechargeable batteries and powerful magnets, and the core of vitamin B12; mischievous, crafty and gifted.

No crown unless the opening line says she wears one; steam, pipes and gauges in the scene.

Nothing slipped off. Intimate areas covered; no corset; keep the costume above, material and palette.

4. SCENE
World: around 1840 at a Saxon blue-colour works near Schneeberg: roasting kilns driving the pale arsenic fumes out of cobalt ore, a glasshouse melting it into deep-blue smalt that is then ground into pigment, a painting room where porcelain painters brush cobalt blue onto white plates.
Pose: standing confidently, her body turned slightly while her face looks toward the viewer.
Light: bright warm sunlight with soft sky light bounced from white clouds.
Composition: vertical 2:3 full-body framing with modest headroom and clear space below the boots — the whole figure from the top of her head or headpiece to both feet stays inside the frame, occupying about four-fifths of the image height, with the same camera distance in every world; her hands stay inside the frame.
